The Ultimate Lake District Motorcycle Loop

This 120-mile circular route takes in the best of the Lake District in a single day. It covers the major passes, skirts the most beautiful lakes, and passes through classic Lakeland villages. Start from Keswick and allow a full day — you'll want to stop constantly.

The Route

Keswick → Honister Pass → Buttermere → Newlands Pass → Whinlatter → Cockermouth → Hardknott Pass → Wrynose Pass → Ambleside → Kirkstone Pass → Ullswater → Keswick. This loop creates a figure-of-eight pattern that maximises the variety of scenery.

Morning Section: Keswick to Buttermere

Leave Keswick early and head south on the B5289 through Borrowdale. This road follows the River Derwent through one of the most beautiful valleys in England. At Seatoller, the road climbs steeply over Honister Pass to Buttermere. Stop at Buttermere village for coffee — the views across the lake are stunning.

Mid-Morning: The Western Passes

From Buttermere, take the Newlands Pass to Braithwaite, then follow the Whinlatter Pass through the forest to Cockermouth. Head south through Ennerdale to pick up the road to Eskdale and the famous Hardknott Pass. This is the most challenging section — 33% gradients and tight hairpins.

The sequence of Hardknott and Wrynose passes back-to-back is one of the greatest motorcycle experiences in England. Allow at least an hour for these 15 miles.

Afternoon: The Eastern Lakes

After conquering Wrynose Pass, descend to Little Langdale and Ambleside. Stop for lunch at one of Ambleside's many pubs — the Golden Rule is a classic. Then tackle the Kirkstone Pass heading north, the Lake District's highest pass at 454 metres. Drop down the other side to the shores of Ullswater.

Evening: Ullswater and Home

The A592 along Ullswater is one of England's most scenic lakeside roads. Gentle bends follow the water's edge with fell views on both sides. At Pooley Bridge, turn west on the A66 for a fast run back to Keswick. You'll arrive tired, exhilarated, and already planning your next visit. Practical Information

  • Distance: Approximately 120 miles
  • Time: 6-8 hours with stops
  • Fuel: Fill up in Keswick or Ambleside. No fuel on the passes
  • Food: Buttermere (morning), Ambleside (lunch), Pooley Bridge (afternoon tea)
  • Best season: May-June or September for quieter roads
  • Avoid: Bank holidays and school summer holidays
keyTakeaways: A 120-mile figure-of-eight loop from Keswick takes in the major passes and lakes in a single day.
The route runs Keswick, Honister, Buttermere, Newlands, Whinlatter, Hardknott, Wrynose, Ambleside, Kirkstone and Ullswater.
The back-to-back Hardknott and Wrynose passes hit 33% gradients and need at least an hour for 15 miles.
Fuel in Keswick or Ambleside as there is none on the passes; allow six to eight hours with stops.
Best ridden May to June or September, avoiding bank holidays and school summer holidays.

faq.q: How long does the Lake District loop take?
faq.a: The full 120-mile figure-of-eight takes six to eight hours with stops. You will want to stop constantly for photos and coffee, so treat it as a full day out from Keswick rather than a quick blast. Allow at least an hour alone for the Hardknott and Wrynose passes.

faq.q: Where can I get fuel and food on the loop?
faq.a: Fill up in Keswick or Ambleside, as there is no fuel on the passes. For food, Buttermere village suits a morning coffee, Ambleside pubs such as the Golden Rule work for lunch, and Pooley Bridge is ideal for afternoon tea before the fast A66 run back to Keswick.

faq.q: When should I ride the circular loop?
faq.a: May to June or September give the quietest roads and most reliable weather. Avoid bank holidays and the school summer holidays, when tourist traffic clogs the narrow passes and turns a flowing ride into a stop-start crawl behind cars and campervans.

faq.q: What is the toughest part of the route?
faq.a: The back-to-back Hardknott and Wrynose passes are the most challenging, with 33% gradients and tight hairpins across roughly 15 miles. It is one of the greatest motorcycle experiences in England, but take your time, use first gear on the steep sections and give way to uphill traffic.
